ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> We recruited couples in the first year of their relationship and followed them over 18 months, with reports every three months.

> This stability is notable given that participants were followed during a period of early relationship development in which sexual and relational experiences are likely in flux.

> The sample included couples with diverse sexual orientations, but most participants were in mixed-gender relationships, and the sample was not large enough to test whether trajectories or associations differed across groups.

> In addition, all participants were living in Canada or the United States, and beliefs about sexuality, relationship development, and relationship maintenance may vary across cultural contexts.

Ethics approval statement:

> The research received ethics approval from our institution.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Do Sexual Beliefs Shape Relationship Quality Over Time? Evidence From Early Romantic Relationships

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								University of Toronto Mississauga

text.text: Satisfying romantic relationships are important for well-being yet are difficult to maintain, as sexual satisfaction and relationship quality often decline across early relationship development.
Sexual growth and destiny beliefs reflect whether sexual satisfaction is viewed as something that develops through effort or depends on natural, inherent compatibility.
Such beliefs may be associated with how couples navigate changes in their relationship.

Using longitudinal data from 161 couples (N= 322) early in their relationship, followed over 18 months, we examined whether individuals' and their partners' sexual beliefs predicted trajectories of sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment.
Relationship satisfaction and commitment showed small declines over time, whereas sexual satisfaction and sexual beliefs remained relatively stable.

Higher actor and partner sexual growth beliefs were associated with higher levels of all outcomes in general, and individuals with partners' higher in sexual growth beliefs were buffered from steeper declines in relationship satisfaction and commitment over time.
In contrast, higher actor, but not partner, sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment in general.

Overall, the findings suggest that sexual beliefs function as relatively stable cognitive frameworks, with partner sexual growth beliefs playing a role in protecting relationship quality and commitment during early relationship development.

text.text: Individuals who report higher sexual satisfaction also tend to report greater relationship satisfaction and commitment (Sprecher, 2002; Sprecher & Cate, 2004), and longitudinal work suggests that changes in sexual satisfaction predict later changes in relationship satisfaction, but not the reverse (Park et al., 2023).

text.text: Given these close links, changes in sexual satisfaction as relationships develop may also be accompanied by changes in broader relationship quality.
Indeed, sexual satisfaction has been shown to increase during the first year of dating and subsequently decline (Schmiedeberg & Schröder, 2016).

text.text: Commitment may follow a somewhat different pattern, with cross-sectional data suggesting progressively higher commitment over the first three years of dating, but lower commitment at longer durations thereafter (Freeman et al., 2023).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that early relationship development is a consequential period of change in sexual and relational experiences, highlighting the importance of identifying factors that are associated with how these trajectories unfold over time.
One such factor may be individuals' lay beliefs about how sexual satisfaction is maintained.
Individuals who endorse sexual growth beliefs view sexual satisfaction as something that can be maintained through effort, communication, compromise, and the resolution of differences.
In contrast, those higher in sexual destiny beliefs view sexual satisfaction as something dependent on inherent compatibility and "natural" sexual chemistry (Maxwell et al., 2017).

text.text: In general, sexual growth beliefs are associated with higher sexual and relationship satisfaction for both partners (Wu & Zheng, 2022), even in the face of sexual disagreements (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2017).

text.text: In contrast, sexual destiny beliefs have been linked to lower sexual and relationship satisfaction, particularly when couples face sexual difficulties or differences, as these challenges are more likely to be interpreted as signs of incompatibility (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2021; Rossi et al., 2022).

text.text: However, we know relatively little about how sexual beliefs change over time as a relationship develops, or how they are associated with trajectories of sexual satisfaction and relationship quality.

To date, sexual growth and destiny beliefs have primarily been studied among individuals in established relationships (Cultice et al., 2021; Maxwell et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2021; Rossi et al., 2022; Uppot et al., 2024; Wu & Zheng, 2022).

In the current study, we examine trajectories of sexual growth and destiny beliefs in couples early in their relationship, followed over 18 months, and test whether sexual growth and destiny beliefs are associated with sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment over time.
Although sexual and relationship satisfaction often decline as relationships progress, the timing and pattern of these changes differ across aspects of relationship quality.

Sexual satisfaction tends to be particularly high early in relationships: in a large longitudinal German panel study, sexual satisfaction increased during the first year of a relationship and then declined (Schmiedeberg & Schröder, 2016).

text.text: Relationship satisfaction also tends to decline over time, with the largest declines occurring during the early years (Bühler et al., 2021) and particularly pronounced declines among relationships that eventually dissolve (Bühler & Orth, 2024).

text.text: Commitment may follow a different pattern, with cross-sectional evidence suggesting higher commitment across the first several years of dating (Freeman et al., 2023).

text.text: These patterns point to a potentially paradoxical feature of early relationship development: partners may become increasingly invested in and motivated to maintain their relationship (Rusbult, 1980 (Rusbult, , 1983)), even as they begin to encounter declines or changes in sexual desire and satisfaction (Frederick et al., 2017; Schmiedeberg & Schröder, 2016).

text.text: How partners interpret these changes may therefore be particularly important.
Declines in sexual desire or satisfaction may be understood as normative challenges that can be navigated together or, alternatively, as signs of deeper incompatibility between partners.

Consistent with this possibility, among women who perceived declines in sexual desire from earlier in their relationships, some described maintaining high relationship quality despite this, whereas others questioned their relationships and reported greater conflict (Moor et al., 2021).

text.text: Given that couples may experience sexual changes such as declines in desire during early relationship development, beliefs about how sexual satisfaction is maintained, rather than beliefs about relationship maintenance more generally, might play a particularly important role in sexual and relationship quality during this time.

That is, sexual growth and destiny beliefs may guide interpretation of sexual changes during this time, shaping how couples respond to such changes and potentially buffering against or exacerbating declines in sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment.
Relatively little is known about how sexual growth and destiny beliefs themselves change over time.

Research on implicit beliefs about relationships more broadly suggests that these beliefs show low to moderate stability over time, with test-retest reliabilities for relationship beliefs ranging from approximately .40 to .74 (Franiuk et al., 2004; Knee, 1998).

text.text: However, we do not yet know whether these beliefs change during the early stages of a relationship or whether they are associated with trajectories of sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment during this period.

Examining these patterns can help clarify whether sexual beliefs function as relatively stable cognitive frameworks that are associated with how couples interpret and respond to sexual and relational changes as more enduring relationship patterns are established.

As sexual growth and destiny beliefs shape how sexual differences and declines are interpreted, they may also be relevant to how partners respond to one another, not only to how each person experiences their own relationship.

Partners higher in sexual growth beliefs may be more likely to view emerging sexual differences as challenges that can be addressed rather than signs of incompatibility, and prior work suggests that growth beliefs are associated with greater responsiveness during sexual challenges (Cultice et al., 2022; Uppot et al., 2024).

text.text: A partners' responses to sexual differences can shape one another's relationship experiences; therefore, a partner's sexual beliefs may be associated with the trajectory of one's own relationship satisfaction and commitment, above and beyond one's own beliefs.

Prior dyadic research has shown that partners' sexual beliefs are associated with sexual and relational experiences (Maxwell et al., 2017; Uppot et al., 2024), but it remains unclear whether a partner's sexual beliefs are associated with how relationship quality unfolds over longer periods of relationship development.

text.text: In the current study, we examine trajectories of sexual growth and destiny beliefs during early relationship development and test how sexual beliefs are associated with sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment.
We recruited couples in the first year of their relationship and followed them over 18 months, with reports every three months.
First, we explored how sexual growth and destiny beliefs change over time.
Next, we examined trajectories of our key outcomes, sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment over time.
We then examined whether sexual beliefs were associated with these outcomes and their trajectories over time.

Finally, we conducted exploratory analyses to test whether one partner's sexual beliefs were associated with changes in relationship quality over time, as well as covariate analyses accounting for general relationship beliefs to examine whether associations with sexual beliefs remained after accounting for general relationship beliefs.

text.text: The current data are from the Experiences in Relationships Overtime Study (EROS), which consisted of seven online surveys: a 60-minute baseline survey and six 45-minute followup surveys administered every 3 months over 18 months.
Recruitment occurred from November 2020 to January 2022.

Eligible couples were those in which both partners agreed to participate, were 18 years or older, in a committed relationship for at least 3 months and less than 15 months, sexually active, and living in Canada or the United States.
We aimed to recruit 200 couples, with recruitment continuing for the duration of the planned recruitment period.
In total, 198 couples (n = 396) completed the baseline survey.
For the current analyses, we included participants who completed at least two time points.

The final sample for the current analyses comprised 161 couples (N= 322); see Table 1 for complete demographic details. ᵃOne couple had been together for 17.5 months at baseline and was included despite slightly exceeding the prespecified eligibility criterion of less than 15 months due to recruitment challenges.

We began by testing the simplest model and incrementally added complexity, ensuring each model ran successfully before proceeding.

text.text: Couples' sexual relationships often change with increasing relationship duration (e.g., Schmiedeberg & Schröder, 2016), yet little was known about how partners' sexual beliefs are associated with these early relationship trajectories.

text.text: In the current study, we followed couples over 18 months as they moved beyond the early stages of their relationship and examined trajectories of sexual beliefs, sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment.
To assess whether these patterns extended beyond beliefs specific to sexuality, we also examined associations with sexual beliefs after accounting for general relationship beliefs.

Sexual growth and destiny beliefs were largely stable over time, with sexual growth beliefs showing significant but very small declines, suggesting that these beliefs may function as relatively stable cognitive frameworks during early relationship development.
At the same time, relationship satisfaction and commitment declined modestly, with small nonlinear trends, whereas sexual satisfaction was stable.
In line with past research (e.g., Maxwell et al., 2017), sexual growth beliefs were consistently associated with more positive sexual and relational outcomes.
text.formatted: In line with past research (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Maxwell et al., 2017)</ref>, sexual growth beliefs were consistently associated with more positive sexual and relational outcomes.

text.text: Individuals who held stronger sexual growth beliefs-and those whose partners held stronger sexual growth beliefsreported higher sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment.

Partner sexual growth beliefs also moderated changes in relationship satisfaction and commitment over time: individuals with partners lower in sexual growth beliefs showed steeper declines in these outcomes, whereas those with partners higher in sexual growth beliefs showed relatively stable levels.
In contrast, sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment but were not associated with changes in outcomes over time.
Sexual destiny beliefs remained stable across the study, whereas sexual growth beliefs showed a small decline over time.

Overall, however, both beliefs demonstrated substantial stability across 18 months, consistent with theoretical perspectives that conceptualize relationship and sexual beliefs as relatively enduring cognitive frameworks that guide how individuals interpret relational experiences (Franiuk et al., 2004; Gander et al., 2025; Knee, 1998; Maxwell et al., 2017).

text.text: This stability is notable given that participants were followed during a period of early relationship development in which sexual and relational experiences are likely in flux.

We also found stability in general relationship growth and destiny beliefs, a finding that diverges from prior research documenting modest increases in relationship growth beliefs and decreases in destiny beliefs over five months among individuals in longer-term relationships (Gander et al., 2025).

text.text: Rather than changing routinely as relationships develop, beliefs may therefore be more likely to shift under particular relational conditions or experiences.

Consistent with this possibility, experimental and intervention research suggests that sexual beliefs can be temporarily shifted (Maxwell et al., 2017; Sutherland & Rehman, 2018), although whether such changes persist is less clear.

text.text: Future research should examine when and under what conditions sexual and relationship beliefs change, including whether more substantial sexual challenges or major relationship transitions are sufficient to reshape these belief systems.
Relationship satisfaction and commitment declined modestly over time, with small quadratic effects indicating that declines were more pronounced earlier in the study and leveling off over time.

The decline in relationship satisfaction is consistent with prior longitudinal work showing particularly pronounced declines during the early years of relationships (Bühler et al., 2021; Bühler & Orth, 2024).

text.text: The decline in commitment differs somewhat from prior crosssectional evidence suggesting higher commitment across the first several years of dating (Freeman et al., 2023) and may reflect some recalibration of relationship evaluations as couples move beyond the highly idealized early stages of relationships and encounter more routine relational experiences (Niehuis et al., 2016).

text.text: Sexual satisfaction, in contrast, remained relatively high and stable across the 18-month study, differing from prior work showing declines with increasing relationship duration (Schiedeberg & Shröder, 2016).

text.text: Because couples in the current study had been together for approximately nine months on average at baseline, we might have expected sexual satisfaction to decline across the follow-up period.
Instead, it remained relatively stable.

Other longitudinal work indicates that sexual satisfaction increases when people enter romantic relationships (Qin et al., 2026), and that sexual activity tends to be more frequent earlier in relationships, when sexual satisfaction is also higher (Schröder & Schmiedeberg, 2015; Yucel & Gassanov, 2010).

text.text: These factors may help explain the relatively high levels of sexual satisfaction observed early in the study, although they do not fully account for its stability across the follow-up period.
Taken together, these findings suggest that sexual and broader relationship outcomes may follow somewhat distinct trajectories during early relationship development.

Relationship satisfaction and commitment declined even while sexual satisfaction remained relatively stable, underscoring the value of examining these dimensions separately rather than assuming that changes in sexual and relationship quality necessarily occur in parallel.

The current findings extend prior research on sexual beliefs by examining how sexual growth and destiny beliefs are associated with sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment over time in early relationships.
Consistent with prior work, higher actor sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment (Maxwell et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2021; Rossi et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with prior work, higher actor sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Maxwell et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Raposo et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Rossi et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, sexual destiny beliefs were not associated with sexual satisfaction and did not predict changes in sexual or relationship outcomes over time.
One possible explanation for these findings is that destiny beliefs become particularly consequential when couples encounter salient sexual challenges.
The absence of an average decline in sexual satisfaction in the present sample may indicate that the couples in our study were not undergoing sexual challenges.

Prior work with couples navigating sexual difficulties or major transitions similarly suggests that sexual destiny beliefs may be especially relevant in the face of sexual issues or incompatibility (Maxwell et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2021; Rossi et al., 2022).

text.text: Future research should examine whether destiny beliefs become more consequential over longer periods of relationship development or during periods of sustained sexual challenge.
Sexual growth beliefs showed a more consistent pattern.

Stronger sexual growth beliefs-both individuals' own and their partners'-were associated with higher sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment, consistent with prior work (Cultice et al., 2022; Maxwell et al., 2017; Raposo et al., 2021).

text.text: Sexual growth beliefs did not, however, predict trajectories of sexual satisfaction, perhaps because sexual satisfaction remained high and stable.

Growth beliefs may instead operate through more proximal processes such as sexual communication, responsiveness to sexual challenges, and motivation to meet a partner's needs (Busby et al., 2024; Uppot et al., 2024; Wu & Zheng, 2022), which could help explain why their dyadic implications extend beyond changes in global sexual satisfaction.

text.text: The clearest evidence that sexual beliefs were associated with change over time emerged for partners' sexual growth beliefs.

Individuals whose partners reported lower sexual growth beliefs showed steeper declines in relationship satisfaction and commitment, whereas those whose partners reported higher sexual growth beliefs showed more stable trajectories.

These findings extend prior work linking sexual growth beliefs to relationship quality (Maxwell et al., 2017) by indicating that a partner's beliefs may be associated with how relationship quality unfolds as couples move through early relationship development.

text.text: Partners higher in sexual growth beliefs may be more likely to view sexual differences as manageable and to respond to them with communication, responsiveness, or continued investment in addressing the problem (Cultice et al., 2022; Uppot et al., 2024; Wu & Zheng, 2022).
text.formatted: Partners higher in sexual growth beliefs may be more likely to view sexual differences as manageable and to respond to them with communication, responsiveness, or continued investment in addressing the problem <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cultice et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Uppot et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Wu & Zheng, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should directly test these interpersonal mechanisms to clarify how one partner's sexual beliefs are associated with the other partner's relationship trajectory.

Despite the strengths of the current longitudinal dyadic design for testing how sexual beliefs are associated with early relationship trajectories, the study was limited in its ability to capture relationship development from the onset of the relationship.
Couples had been together for between three months and just over one year at baseline, and many had likely already established important relational and sexual patterns by the start of the study.
In addition, some couples were already cohabiting, engaged, or married, suggesting that the sample may not fully capture the earliest changes that occur as romantic relationships first form.

To better understand early relationship development, future research could follow individuals before or at the very beginning of relationship formation, although this type of design is difficult to implement (Eastwick & Joel, 2025).
text.formatted: To better understand early relationship development, future research could follow individuals before or at the very beginning of relationship formation, although this type of design is difficult to implement <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Eastwick & Joel, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A second limitation concerns the generalizability of the findings.

The sample included couples with diverse sexual orientations, but most participants were in mixed-gender relationships, and the sample was not large enough to test whether trajectories or associations differed across groups.

Prior research suggests that many sexual and relational processes are similar across mixed-sex and same-sex couples, although some differences have been observed in sexual desire, communication, and satisfaction (Holmberg & Blair, 2009).
text.formatted: Prior research suggests that many sexual and relational processes are similar across mixed-sex and same-sex couples, although some differences have been observed in sexual desire, communication, and satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Holmberg & Blair, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Future research with larger and more diverse samples is needed to test whether the current findings generalize across different relationship structures and orientations.
In addition, all participants were living in Canada or the United States, and beliefs about sexuality, relationship development, and relationship maintenance may vary across cultural contexts.

Future work should examine whether sexual growth and destiny beliefs show similar trajectories and associations with relationship quality in non-Western contexts and in cultures with different norms surrounding sexuality and romantic relationships.
Attrition analyses provided relatively little evidence of systematic dropout, although some selective retention was evident.
Participants retained longer tended to report higher growth beliefs, and those who dropped out reported lower relationship satisfaction at 12 months.

Later waves may therefore somewhat overrepresent more growth-oriented and satisfied participants, potentially contributing to the apparent levelling off in relationship satisfaction at later assessments.

However, the attrition analyses did not directly test whether selective retention influenced the associations between sexual beliefs and changes in relationship quality, including the partner sexual growth belief effects.
Thus, the direction and magnitude of any bias in these longitudinal associations remain unclear.

Future longitudinal research should assess relationship dissolution and reasons for attrition to better distinguish true stabilization in relationship quality from selective retention of more satisfied couples.
The current findings also point to potential directions for interventions.

Prior work suggests that sexual beliefs can be temporarily shifted through brief interventions (Maxwell et al., 2017), raising the possibility that helping couples adopt stronger sexual growth beliefs could support sexual and relational well-being.
However, given the correlational nature of the present findings, future research is needed to test whether fostering sexual growth beliefs leads to improvements in relationship quality over time.

Such work would benefit from dyadic designs that target both partners' beliefs and examine whether changes in sexual growth beliefs promote more adaptive interpersonal processes, such as sexual communication, mindfulness, or motivation to meet a partner's needs (Cultice et al., 2022; Wu & Zheng, 2022; Uppot et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Such work would benefit from dyadic designs that target both partners' beliefs and examine whether changes in sexual growth beliefs promote more adaptive interpersonal processes, such as sexual communication, mindfulness, or motivation to meet a partner's needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cultice et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Wu & Zheng, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Uppot et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such studies could clarify whether sexual growth beliefs play a causal role in maintaining relationship satisfaction and commitment during early relationship development.
The present study provides one of the first longitudinal dyadic tests of sexual growth and destiny beliefs across early relationship development.

Across 18 months, sexual beliefs were relatively stable (showed significant, but very small declines), suggesting that beliefs about how sexual satisfaction is maintained may shape how partners understand and navigate their sexual relationships.
These beliefs were also meaningfully linked to both partners' experiences.

Sexual growth beliefs-both individuals' own and their partners'-were associated with higher sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment, whereas sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment.

Most notably, partners' sexual growth beliefs were associated with trajectories of relationship quality: individuals with partners higher in sexual growth beliefs showed more stable relationship satisfaction and commitment over time.
Thus, sexual beliefs may matter not only for how individuals experience their relationships at a given point in time, but also for how relationship quality unfolds between partners.

As couples move beyond the earliest stages of their relationships, having a partner who views a satisfying sexual relationship as something that can be cultivated may be particularly relevant for sustaining relationship quality over time.
